brief.desc: Bearish, 28 of 100. Friday's 0.16% GLD bounce is a pause one step off a fresh 52-week low, not a turn: the Fed is now pricing a December hike after a hot October CPI, real yields jumped 12bp in a day, and GLD sits 6.7% under its 50-day average. High confidence on direction, low on speed.
brief.yr: GLD closed at 355.45 on November 13, up 0.16%, in a 354.41 to 357.32 range, after Thursday's 2.82% drop to a 52-week low of 352.91. Kitco spot gold finished up 0.18% near 3,884. The decisive moves came earlier in the week: October core CPI beat at 0.3%, the 2-year jumped 17bp and the 10-year real yield 12bp on November 10, and gold broke 4,000 on November 11. GLD fell 4.58% on the week; Friday was weekend short-covering, not buying.
brief.to: Base case (50%) is a grind lower toward 340 on GLD if retail sales on November 17 and Fed speakers keep a 50bp December hike in play; a relief range back toward 370 (35%) needs Fed speakers to settle on 25bp; capitulation toward 325 (15%) needs a 50bp hike to become the base case before the December 8-9 FOMC. This week's calendar is retail sales, FOMC minutes and Fed speakers, with the next CFTC report the key positioning check. This view flips bullish if the 10-year TIPS real yield closes back below 2.60% on a Fed signal that December is the last hike.

brief.why: The October CPI beat on core for the second straight month, breaking the pause narrative that had carried gold off its late-October lows. Governor Waller then opened the door to 50bp at the December 8-9 meeting, and the front end repriced: the 2-year rose from 4.56% to 4.73% on November 10 and futures moved to a fully priced December hike. Because breakevens did not rise with nominal yields, falling 11bp over 20 days to 2.24%, the whole move landed on real yields, and the 10-year TIPS yield climbed back to 2.78%, undoing a month of relief in one print. Rising real yields with falling breakevens is the worst mix for gold: no inflation-hedge bid and a higher carry cost. The dollar compounds it, up 0.85% in four sessions as rate differentials widened. The counterweight is real but slow: official-sector buying of 321 tonnes in Q3 and record ETF holdings at end-October explain why gold did not fall harder, but that demand is price-insensitive and does not respond to a CPI print. The marginal seller is the macro fund repricing the Fed, and short-term ETF flows have turned negative. Until core inflation cools or the Fed signals December is the last hike, the path is lower, though with GLD 30% off its high and on its 52-week low, the easy part of the fall is done.
brief.cons: The loud story is that Fed hikes broke gold below 4,000, and it is right on direction. Where it looks stretched: a December hike is priced at 100% with a 50bp tail, so the hawkish news is largely in the price, and a plain 25bp hike with neutral guidance would be a relief event. GLD is 0.72% above its 52-week low and down 6.95% in 20 days, where short-term shorts get crowded. The bearish trade is now the consensus trade, which is the main risk to this call over days rather than weeks. Positioning is blind: the newest CFTC report is as of October 20, showing Managed Money net long 104,206 contracts, before both the CPI and the break of 4,000, so nobody knows how short funds are now.
fals: Soften: October retail sales on November 17 miss and the 2-year falls back below 4.60% by November 20; the 50bp tail dies and the score moves to the mid-30s.
Invert: the 10-year TIPS real yield closes back below 2.60% on a Fed signal that December is the last hike; the call flips bullish, visible on FRED within one or two business days.

Weak joint: the view assumes funds are not already heavily short and ETF outflows continue, but the newest CFTC data is from October 20 and the outflow figure is one unsourced line; if the next CFTC report shows Managed Money flat or net short, the downside is spent.
